# Iteration

In this week's lesson, we will be talking about how to do repetitive tasks.

As it turns out, computers are really good at repeating tasks. We call this repetition of the same task "iteration."

There are many ways to iterate in R (we will look at a few others at the end of the lesson), but this week focuses on loops, which give us complete control over any kind of repetition we want. Specifically, we will use `for` loops, which perform the same action for each item in a list of things.

## The `for` Loop

The general structure of a `for` loop is below:

```{r}
# for (item in list_of_items) {
#   do_something(item)
# }
```

To see an example of this, let's calculate biomasses from volumes using a loop. If we want to see the results of the loop, we need to print them out.

```{r}
# vector of volumes
volumes <- c(1.6, 3, 8)

# for each volume value in a vector of volumes
for (vol in volumes){           # perform some task inside the {}
  biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9   # calculate a mass
  print(biomass)                # print out the mass
}
```

The code inside the curly brackets runs once for each value in `volumes`. The `vol` object is a placeholder, representing one value from `volumes` at a time.

The loop takes the first value from `volumes`, assigns it to `vol`, and runs everything inside the curly brackets from top to bottom. Then it starts over with the second value, and so on, until it has run through every element.

Ultimately, the loop above is doing the exact same thing as the code below, but in a more condensed and more flexible way.

```{r}
# same as the for loop above
vol <- volumes[1]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[2]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)

vol <- volumes[3]
biomass <- 2.65 * vol ^ 0.9
print(biomass)
```

## Looping with an Index and Storing Results

The loop above uses each value directly; this is called *looping by value*.

There is another way to loop: *looping by index*. Remember sub-setting by index (position) from the beginning of the course? Looping by index loops through position numbers (1, 2, 3...) and uses them to pull values out of a vector with square brackets.

- We often use `i` (for "index") as the placeholder.
- We use `1:length(volumes)` so the loop works no matter how many values there are. (For a data frame, we use `nrow()`.)

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){       # i takes the values 1, 2, 3
  biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9  # volumes[i] is the ith volume
  print(biomass)
}
```

Same result, but more complicated to read. So why loop by index? The most common reason is to store the results in the same order (position) as the values we used to calculate them.

To store results, we create an empty object *before* the loop starts. The `vector()` function makes an empty vector:

- `mode` is the type of data we are going to store
- `length` is the number of items in the vector

```{r}
biomasses <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(volumes))
biomasses
```

Then, each trip through the loop, we put the output into the `i`th position of the empty vector.

```{r}
for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomass <- 2.65 * volumes[i] ^ 0.9
   biomasses[i] <- biomass
}

biomasses
```

Looping by index also lets us pull values from several vectors at the same position.

```{r}
a_values <- c(2.65, 1.28, 3.29)
b_values <- c(0.9, 1.1, 1.2)

for (i in 1:length(volumes)){
   biomasses[i] <- a_values[i] * volumes[i] ^ b_values[i]
}

biomasses
```

## Looping over Data Frames

Several vectors of the same length, lined up by position...that is exactly what the columns of a data frame are! Most of the time, the values you want to loop over will be in a data frame.

```{r}
data <- data.frame(a = a_values, b = b_values, volume = volumes)
data
```

To loop over rows, we loop by index from 1 to `nrow()`, and use `$` plus `[i]` to grab the value in a specific column for that row. To store results, we can create a new, empty column first.

This is also where loops really shine: we can put an `if`-`else` statement inside a loop. Let's only calculate biomass if the volume is less than 5.

```{r}
data$biomass <- NA   # new, empty column

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    biomass <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  data$biomass[i] <- biomass
}

data
```

We can also call a function inside a loop. Remember that functions containing `if`-`else` statements are not vectorized, so we can't just give them a whole column; a loop solves that.

```{r}
est_biomass <- function(volume, a, b){
  if (volume < 5) {
    biomass <- a * volume ^ b
  } else {
    biomass <- NA
  }
  return(biomass)
}

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  data$biomass[i] <- est_biomass(data$volume[i], data$a[i], data$b[i])
}

data
```

> Do you need a loop? For a calculation within a single data frame, the tidyverse way is usually simpler. `if_else()` is vectorized, so it works inside `mutate()` with no loop:
>
> ```{r}
> data |>
>   dplyr::mutate(biomass = dplyr::if_else(volume < 5, a * volume ^ b, NA))
> ```
>
> Loops are most useful when the repetition goes *beyond* one data frame, such as performing multiple complicated tasks or working through many files (coming up next!). We'll see more alternatives to loops at the end of the lesson.

## Troubleshooting Loops

Occasionally (okay, maybe often...) when you write a for loop, it will either give you an error or run successfully but give results you didn't anticipate.

Since loops have a placeholder in them (such as `i`), the best way to figure out what is going on is to set the placeholder equal to a specific value and run each line of code between the `{}` one at a time.

What is wrong with the loop below?

```{r}
#| eval: false
data$biomass <- NA

for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
  if (data$volume[i] < 5) {
    data$biomass[i] <- data$a[i] * data$volume[i] ^ data$b[i]
  } else {
    data$biomass <- NA
  }
}

data

# in the console, set i to a number; run the code inside the loop line by line
# i <- 2
# i <- 3
```

If part of your loop is working but another part isn't, find a value (or row) that should trigger the part that isn't working and set the index to that.

## Looping over Files

Loops are especially handy when we have many similar files and want to do the same tasks to each one.

To demonstrate, let's download some simulated satellite collar data. Make sure you change the file paths to match the sub-directories in your RStudio Project, as needed.

```{r}
download.file(url = "http://www.datacarpentry.org/semester-biology/data/locations.zip",
              destfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip") # where to put the zip file

# zipfile argument is the location of the file to be unzipped
# exdir argument is the location where the "extracted" files should be placed
unzip(zipfile = "../data_raw/locations.zip", exdir = "../data_raw/")
```

Before we can loop through these files, we need their names. The `list.files()` function lists the files in a directory. The optional `pattern` argument lets us keep only the files we want (and can take regular expressions).

```{r}
# in regex, .* means any character (.) any number of times (*)
# "locations.*.txt" indicates any file starting with "locations" and ending with ".txt"
data_files <- list.files(path = "../data_raw/", pattern = "locations.*.txt")
data_files
```

Let's say we want the file name, the number of observations, and the minimum latitude for each file. Since we are collecting several pieces of information, we'll store them in a data frame.

We start by creating an empty data frame with `data.frame()`. Each argument is one column: `column_name` = an empty vector of the correct type and length.

```{r}
num_files <- length(data_files)

results <- data.frame(file_name = vector(mode = "character", length = num_files),
                      count = vector(mode = "integer", length = num_files),
                      min_lat = vector(mode = "numeric", length = num_files))
results
```

Then we loop over the files, read each one in, and store the information in the `i`th row of the appropriate column.

```{r}
for (i in 1:num_files){

  # read in the data file
  filename <- data_files[i]
  locations <- read.csv(paste0("../data_raw/", filename))

  # add information about the data file into the data frame
  results$file_name[i] <- filename
  results$count[i] <- nrow(locations)
  results$min_lat[i] <- min(locations$lat)

}

results
```

## Other Ways to Iterate

Loops aren't the only way to repeat things in R. In fact, we have been iterating all semester without calling it that!

- Vectorized functions: most functions (including the ones we wrote in Week 11) work on a whole vector at once. The exception is functions with `if`-`else` statements inside them.
- `dplyr` functions: `mutate()`, `filter()`, and friends repeat a calculation for every row of a data frame. To use a function with `if`-`else` inside `mutate()`, add `rowwise()` first.
- `apply` and `map` functions: apply a function to each item in a list. The `apply` family (`sapply`, `lapply`, etc.) is base R; the `map` family comes from the `purrr` package in the `tidyverse`. See the [`purrr` cheatsheet](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/) or [Chapter 26: Iteration](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/iteration) in "R for Data Science (2e)" if you are curious.

Here is a function with an `if`-`else` inside, used on every value without writing a loop:

```{r}
size_class <- function(volume){
  if (volume < 5) {
    size <- "small"
  } else {
    size <- "large"
  }
  return(size)
}

# sapply() runs the function on each value and returns a vector
sapply(volumes, size_class)

# rowwise() lets mutate() run the function one row at a time
data |>
  dplyr::rowwise() |>
  dplyr::mutate(size = size_class(volume))
```
